newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress begins meeting to try to avert poll.
newsitem.headline: India Congress begins meeting to try to avert poll.

text.p: India's battle-weary Congress party, trying to avert early polls after toppling caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition government last week, began a key meeting on Monday to find a successor.

Party sources said Congress president Sitaram Kesri would make a formal offer of support for Deve Gowda's United Front alliance to allow it to make a fresh bid to form a government with a new leader at the helm.
Deve Gowda broke a political logjam on Sunday when he told his 15-party coalition that he would meet Congress's demand and step down if his partners so decided.
"G.K. Moopanar fits the bill quite nicely," one Kesri aide told Reuters, referring to the head of caretaker Finance Minister P.Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress, a regional party.
"Talks will be held soon," the aide said. "We hope he will agree in the national interest. We must avoid elections at any cost."
Moopanar, is a publicity-shy Tamil politician close to Sonia Gandhi, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi's Italian-born widow who also wields considerable influence with Kesri.
Congress said earlier on Monday the nation's political crisis could end in a week as the ousted United Front alliance stepped up efforts to find a successor to Deve Gowda.
Until Sunday, Deve Gowda and his partners had refused to bow to Congress's demand that the coalition change leaders before a new government could be formed.
"We have to keep the national interest above everything else," said United Front leader Chandrababu Naidu, considered a leading contender to succeed Deve Gowda as prime minister.
"Why should the nation pay for our rigid stands?... The institution is important, not individuals."

Deve Gowda's reversal opened the door to a possible new alignment, with Congress supporting a fresh governing coalition led by the United Front and strongly resembling the centre-left team that fell last week.
It also dramatically reduced the prospects -- at least for now -- of mid-term polls that could benefit Hindu nationalists.
Congress, which provoked Deve Gowda's downfall last Friday by withdrawing its support for his 10-month-old government, welcomed the caretaker prime minister's move.
"If they have any other leader, we are prepared to support them," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said.
Asked how long it would take the United Front and Congress to work out a new deal, Gadgil said: "About a week."
The United Front, due to meet on Thursday to choose a new chief, said it had deferred the meeting to April 20.

Apart from Andhra Pradesh state Chief Minister Naidu, who said he was not interested, Moopanar, Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Industry Minister Murasoli Maran, a member of the Tamil group, were reported to be in the fray.

Newspapers said Monday's meeting of the Congress Working Committee was shaping up as a battle between Kesri and the party's leader in the lower house, Sharad Pawar, who has given lukewarm support to the move to topple Deve Gowda.
While the United Front said it was open to forming a fresh coalition under a new leader, it expressed concern over the "credibility" and "durability" of Congress' support.
"That is a matter of negotiation," Gadgil said.

The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is parliament's biggest party with 162 seats in the 542-member lower house. With its allies it controls 193 votes, ahead of the United Front's 178 and Congress's 140.
